title: What is known about 1RB0LE_1LC0RE_0RA0LD_1LA1LF_0LC0RA_0LB---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LE_1LC0RE_0RA0LD_1LA1LF_0LC0RA_0LB---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state machine halts from blank tape. It belongs to a family of six holdouts with almost the same table (F0 = 0LB, E1 = 0RA). Their tapes are made of the words 10 and 110, grouped in sections split by 000, and they grow slowly to the left. This page lists what has been established, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The engine is decoded and proved in Lean for every size and every layout. At an event the tape is a base-3 counter N, then a binary counter Z, then a chain of binary words; N and Z get 1 per event, and every word is a counter that, when it wraps, sends 3 to the next word (so a carry is multiplied by 3 at every separator, and an empty word passes 3 times what it got). This chain law covers every layout the run has shown (the plain cascade, the X layer and all later eras are special cases) and is proved in lean/Layers.lean for any number of words of any widths. Inside a layout the whole right side is one number that grows by 1 per event, so an era change happens only when a carry runs off the last word. Using this, a simulator that jumps from one era change to the next and runs each change cell by cell has followed the run through 510 changes of era, 2.4·10297 events (so at least that many steps), with no halt. What an era change hands on (the new widths and values, and how many base-3 digits it takes from N) is the open part; C never runs out of digits: instead the chain keeps gaining words.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 178 cells have been visited and 70 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Sweep rules
claims.text: The head crosses runs of the words 01, 10, 011 or 110 in one state, rewriting each copy the same way, for any number of copies and any surrounding tape.

claims.title: No halt in 3·10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator runs 3·10<sup>9</sup> steps without a halt.

claims.title: Where it can halt
claims.text: A closed tape language with windows of 6 cells (closed, found and checked by bbtools.ctl, not yet in Lean) allows a halt only with F reading a 1 and 110000, 110001, 110101 from the head on: the first 1 of a word 110 followed by a section break 000 1.

claims.title: The first section
claims.text: At its visits to the left end (in state E) the tape starts E>0 0 1 0 (1 1 0)^k …; the record values of k: 11 at step 31,482,224, 12 at step 56,276,639, 13 at step 138,079,678, 14 at step 271,307,991, 15 at step 645,244,842, 16 at step 1,767,055,517. Its first 21 left-end configurations also occur in the run of 1RB0LE_1LC0RE_0RA0LD_1LA1LF_0LC0RA_0LE---; later the two runs differ.

claims.title: Growth
claims.text: Each new 110 at the front costs about 2 to 3 times the steps of the previous one, the signature of a counter; the rest of the tape changes everywhere between visits, so the counter's digits are not simply blocks.

claims.title: The event rule, for every size
claims.text: From an event 0^∞ 1 0 [N] A> 0 [M] 1 [R] (N base 3 in 3-cell digits 100/110/010, M and R binary in 4-cell digits 0010/1010 and 1000/1010, low digit first) the machine reaches the next event with N + 1, M + 1 and, when M wraps, R + 3; 54 theorems, one per case (54 cases, exhaustive by construction of events.py, not by a Lean theorem; carries over k twos in N, i ones in M, j ones in R; the wrap of N at the left end), each with its exact step count and any tape beyond.

claims.title: The run follows the rule
claims.text: The run reaches the clean shape (R followed by 1 0 1 and blank tape) at step 7,591 (N = 4 (2 digits), M = 2 (2 digits), R = 2 (8 digits)); 433 consecutive events then follow the rule, until the first overflow of R (8 digits, R = 254, at about step 20,500). Counting all events of the form N, 0 [M] 1, anything: 5,820 of the first 3·106 steps follow from the previous one by the rule, 1,045 do not (wraps of M that reach the undecoded part).

claims.title: Token rows of the visit law
claims.text: Vis q x r x': the head enters the stream x from the left in state q and first leaves it to the left in state r, leaving x'. With tokens of two cells right of the event cell, 29 rows occur in 3·107 steps; each is a Lean theorem, conditional on the nested visits of the rest of the stream and valid for every stream.

claims.title: The a/z stream and M as a recursive visit law
claims.text: Everything from R on, blank tape included, is one stream of a = 10 and z = 00. A visit in state B turns the first z into a and every second a before it into z; it comes out in A when the first z is at an odd place (the binary increment of R, for every size: vb_odd, ve_odd) and in C when it is at an even place (vb_even). M + 1 without a wrap (m_inc) and with a wrap, where the stream gets three visits (m_wrap), for every size.

claims.title: The overflow of R is the even case of the stream law
claims.text: R has no end: when all its digits up to the blank tape are 1, the first z is at an even place and the visit comes out in C, leaving the digits shifted by one token. In the run of 1RB0LE_1LC0RE_0RA0LD_1LA1LF_0LC0RA_0LB--- this first happens at step 20,645 (stream a18 then blank, left as (z a)9 a). That the event rule fails only there is read off the rules, not a Lean theorem.

claims.title: The cascade rule of the later layout, for every size
claims.text: From an event 0^∞ 1 0 [N] A> 0 [Z] 1 1 [C] 0 1 [R] (N base 3 as before; Z, the former M, in 4-cell digits 0010/1010; C binary in 4-cell digits 0001 = 0, 0101 = 1; R as before; lowest digit first) the machine reaches the next event with N + 1, Z + 1, C + 3 when Z wraps and R + 3 when C wraps; 162 theorems, one per case, each with its exact step count.

claims.title: The chain law, for every layout
claims.text: At an event the right side is 0∞ 1 0 [N] A> 0 [Z] 1 1 [W₁] 0 1 [U₁] 1 0 1 1 [W₂] 0 1 [U₂] … 1 0 1 1 [Wm] 0 1 [Um] 0∞: Z (digits 0010, 1010), each W (0001, 0101) and each U (1000, 1010) binary, lowest digit first, of any width, W and U possibly empty, any number m of pairs. From one event to the next: N + 1, Z + 1; when Z wraps, W₁ gets 3; each wrap of a W gives its U 3; each wrap of a U gives the next W 3, as long as no carry leaves the last word. Equivalently Z + 2|Z|/3 · (W₁ + 2|W₁|/3 · (U₁ + 2|U₁|/3 · (W₂ + …))) grows by exactly 1 per event. 23 visit rows (24 for E1 = 0RE) of blocks of 1, 2 and 4 cells, composed by induction over the digits of each word and over the list of pairs; the generator is this family's copy of the one first written for 1RB---_1LC0RF_0RA0LD_1LE1LA_1RF0LF_0LC0RA.

claims.title: The run follows the chain law
claims.text: In the first 200,000,000 steps, 5,386,399 pairs of consecutive full events in one layout follow the law (the number above gains exactly 1), with no mismatch; 10 pairs change the layout (changes of era), 32 full events are in no layout.

claims.title: No halt through the first changes of era
claims.text: The simulator runs the machine cell by cell from blank tape; at each full event in a layout it computes from the chain law the last event before a carry would leave the last word, writes that tape and runs on cell by cell through the change of era. 510 changes of era, 2.4·10<sup>297</sup> events in all (each at least one step), 7,770,361 steps run cell by cell, no halt; at the end the chain has 25 words, 1024 digits in all. Before each jump it checks the law on random events of the era, rebuilt and run cell by cell: 101,238 events, 0 mismatches. Rests on the chain law (Lean) and on the simulator's arithmetic (the number above, decoded back into words), which is not in Lean.

claims.title: What a change of era hands on
claims.text: At the end of an era the words are at or near their largest values; after the change they hold small values, the boundaries between words have moved by a digit, the last word has one digit more, and N has either gained 1 (the change is one event, and two words disappear) or lost 2 to 9 base-3 digits, depending on N mod 9 and more, which become new words. A rule for this hand-over, and whether a change of era can ever halt, are open.

claims.title: The run follows the cascade
claims.text: Every one of the 4,866,936 full events (the tape left of the head exactly 0^∞ 1 0 [N]) from step 173,166,400 to 3·108 has the plain layout with Z, C, R of 10, 4 and 17 digits, and each follows from the one before by the rule, with no mismatch; N grows from 14 to 15 digits at step 271,308,046.

claims.title: Eras with an extra word X
claims.text: Before step 173,166,400 (and after step 53,170) the full events carry one more word, c a X in tokens with X a short binary word, between Z and C: Z, X, C, R of widths 3, 1, 7, 14 (steps 3,216,980 to 20,188,680), 4, 2, 6, 15 (to 58,840,416), 5, 3, 5, 16 (to 173,165,846); then X is gone and the plain layout has widths 10, 4, 17. From step 3.2 million each change of era takes a digit from C and gives one to R (their widths add up to 21).

claims.title: The X layer, for every size
claims.text: In the layout 0^∞ 1 0 [N] A> 0 [Z] 1 1 0 1 1 0 [X] 1 1 [C] 0 1 [R], with X a binary word of k = 1, 2 or 3 digits written like Z, an event in which Z wraps gives X + 1 (mod 2k) and C + 24/2k, 3 more when X wraps, and R + 3 when C wraps: 2kC + 3X gains 27. 441 theorems in two parts glued by steps_add: the right side (every X, C's low digits written out, any carry, every width of Z, C and R), then N + 1 for every tape on the right. Events in which Z does not wrap are the rules of Cascade.lean.

claims.title: The run follows the X layer
claims.text: All 4,349,409 consecutive pairs of full events in the X layout in the first 3·10<sup>8</sup> steps follow this law (207,143 with k = 1, 828,445 with k = 2, 3,313,821 with k = 3), with no mismatch.

claims.title: The changes of era
claims.text: At steps 20,189,536, 58,841,166 and 173,166,400 a wrap of Z carries through C into R and R + 3 reaches 2<sup>width</sup> or more: R gets a digit more, C loses one, X gains one (the last time X disappears and Z grows from 5 to 10 digits). At the first two, N loses its two lowest digits to the words on the right (124,490 + 1 = 9·13,832 + 3, then N = 13,833; 54,958 + 1 = 9·6,106 + 5, then N = 6,107). The exact values before and after are listed in the README.

claims.title: An era change mixes N into the binary words
claims.text: Each of the last three changes of era is one step from a full event to the next (554 to 856 steps); the tape of step 173,165,846, built by hand, reaches the values of the run. With X, Z, C and R fixed, the outcome depends on N mod 9: for N mod 9 = 1, 2, 4, 5 the X layout returns with two digits of N moved into Z, otherwise three or more digits of N are taken and the shape is new.

claims.title: No halt near 20,412 hand-built era changes
claims.text: Every era change with Z of 2 to 4 digits, X of 0 to 3 digits, C of 5 digits about to wrap, R of 6 digits about to overflow and N from 81 to 107, followed for 12 events: none halts.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows whether it halts. Its engine is decoded and proved: a base-3 counter on the left and a chain of binary words on the right tick together, and each word that wraps sends 3 to the next. So between two changes of era the whole right side is one counter. A simulator built on this has followed the run for 2.4·10<sup>297</sup> events without a halt; what a change of era hands on is the open question.

facts.text: The chain law (each wrap sends 3 to the next word), in Lean.
Events of the run (510 eras followed), no halt.
The event rule (N+1, M+1, R+3 on a wrap) for every size, in Lean.
Events by the rule in 3·10<sup>6</sup> steps.

Consecutive events by the cascade rule from step 173 million to 3·10<sup>8</sup>, no mismatch.
The X layer (X + 1, C + 24/2<sup>k</sup>, 3 more when X wraps) in Lean.

sections.heading: Three counters on one tape
html: At the moments we call events (the head in state A, on a 0, just right of the left counter) the tape reads
0∞ 1 0 [N] A> 0 [M] 1 [R] …

• N, a base-3 counter: 3-cell digits 100 = 0, 110 = 1, 010 = 2, most significant first, its lowest digit next to the head;
  • M, a binary counter: 4-cell digits 0010 = 0, 1010 = 1, lowest digit first (next to the head);
  • R, a second binary counter after a single 1: 4-cell digits 1000 = 0, 1010 = 1, lowest digit first.
In the words a = 10, b = 110 of the older description, M's digits read as sections a| and aa, which is why the tape looked like sections of a's split by 000.

sections.heading: One event: N + 1, M + 1, and R + 3 when M wraps
html: From one event to the next the head runs right over M (and over R only when M wraps), comes back, crawls into N, adds one there and returns. The net effect:

counterchange per event
N+1 in base 3; trailing 2s carry; when N = 2…2 it becomes 0…0 with one digit more (the tape grows 3 cells at the left)
M+1 in binary; trailing 1s carry; from 1…1 it wraps to 0…0 (same width)
Runchanged, except when M wraps: then +3 in binary

So N counts events (mod 3width), M counts them mod 2width, and R gains 3 every 2width of M events: two different bases running side by side. Example from the run of 1RB0LE_1LC0RE_0RA0LD_1LA1LF_0LC0RA_0LB--- (M with 2 digits, R with 8): at steps 12,203, 12,223, 12,243, 12,253, 12,345 the triple (N, M, R) is (5, 0, 92), (6, 1, 92), (7, 2, 92), (8, 3, 92), (9, 0, 95).

Each case of this rule is a theorem in lean/Events.lean, proved for every size: 9 cases for N (lowest digit 0 or 1 after 0, 1 or k+2 twos, or the wrap of 2…2 at the left end), times 6 for M and R (no wrap, carry over i+1 ones, or a wrap of M with i+1 digits combined with the 4 cases of R's two low bits and a carry over j ones). 54 cases (exhaustive by construction of events.py), one theorem each, with its exact step count, e.g. 12i + 12j + 10k + 116 steps for a carry over k twos in N, a wrap of M with i+1 digits and R ending in 10 followed by j ones. When M does not wrap, nothing right of M is read, so these rules hold whatever lies beyond.

sections.heading: How long the run keeps this shape
html: In the clean shape R is followed by 1 0 1 and blank tape. This run reaches it at step 7,591 (N = 4 (2 digits), M = 2 (2 digits), R = 2 (8 digits)) and then 433 consecutive events follow the rule, until the first overflow of R (8 digits, R = 254, at about step 20,500).

An overflow of R (its carry running into the cells after it) is not covered by the rules: there the head goes past R and rebuilds the right part; in 1RB0LE_1LC0RE_0RA0LD_1LA1LF_0LC0RA_0LB--- the transition D1 (the only way into F, whose 1 halts) is used in the first 105 steps only at steps 138, 1,008, 3,177, 7,571 (before the clean shape) and 20,756, 53,353, 92,444, 92,861 (at the first three overflows of R). After the first overflows the cells right of R are no longer just 1 0 1: they hold a further structure starting 1 0 1 1 0 …, and M and R take other widths. Counting every event whose left part is N and whose right part starts 0 [M] 1, 5,820 events in the first 3·106 steps follow from the previous one by the rule and 1,045 do not (the wraps of M that touch the undecoded part); at step 3·106: N = 2,159 (8 digits), M with 3 digits.

sections.heading: Two words and a separator
html: Write a for 1 0 and b for 1 1 0. Apart from a few cells at the ends, the tape is a string of a's and b's broken into sections by extra 0s (0 0 0 between two 1s). At its visits to the left end the first section is a b b … b followed by a's and b's, and the later sections are mostly runs of a's. Writing 1 for a and 2 for b, the tape at step 645,244,842 of the first sibling is 1222222222222222 | 111 | 111 | 11111 | 111 | 12 | 11111112 | 111111111 | 11111 | 11111 | 1 | 111 | 1 | 11.

sections.heading: Sweeps and an inner counter
html: The head moves through runs of words in one state, rewriting each copy the same way, for example A turning 0 1 1 into 1 0 0 or B turning 1 0 into 0 1 (proved in Lean for any number of copies: a_right_01, a_right_011, b_right_10, b_right_110, e_right_10). Its excursions do not usually reach the ends: the turning points far from the left end follow the ruler pattern of a binary counter with digits four cells wide (in a stretch of 17,000 steps from step 28,601 of the first sibling the far turning points are 43, 47, 43, 51, 43, 47, 43, 55, … cells from the left end). The ends are visited rarely, and each visit to the left end finds the whole tape rearranged.

sections.heading: Six siblings
html: Five of the six differ only in E1 and F0 (F1 halts in all of them); F is entered only from D reading 1, so F0 runs every time D finds a 1, and the five really are different machines. The sixth is a relabelled relative. All six show the same tape language and the same slow front.

sections.heading: Where it could halt
html: The machine halts only when F reads a 1. A closed tape language with windows of six cells (an over-approximation of every configuration reachable from blank tape, found and checked by bbtools.ctl) allows that only with 110000, 110001, 110101 from the head on: F on the first 1 of a word 1 1 0 that ends a section. Whether the run ever puts F there is the open question.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.051). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 178 cells (139 left of the start, 35 right), with a density of 1s of 0.393.

The tape (run-length coded, 1^5 is five 1s, C>0 the head in state C on a 0) at some of the last moments the head reached a new cell, cut to 400 characters:

sections.heading: A cascade of binary counters, in eras
html:
After the first overflows of R a counter C appears between M and R. In its plain form an event reads

0∞ 1 0 [N] A> 0 [Z] 1 1 [C] 0 1 [R] 0∞

with N in base 3 as before, Z the counter called M above, a new binary counter C (4-cell digits 0001 = 0, 0101 = 1) and R as before. The rule becomes a cascade: every event adds 1 to N and to Z; when Z wraps, C gets 3; when C wraps, R gets 3. That is 162 cases, each a Lean theorem with its exact step count, and the same for all six siblings.

From step 173,166,400 to the end of a 3·108-step run every full event has this plain layout (Z of 10 digits, C of 4, R of 17), and each follows from the one before by the rule: 4,866,936 events, no mismatch.
Before that the run passes through eras with one more short binary word X (c a X in tokens) between Z and C. Each change of era gives R a digit and takes one from C:

The X layer is now decoded and proved in Lean. When Z wraps, X gets 1 and C gets 24/2k (k the number of digits of X), and 3 more when X wraps: so 2kC + 3X gains 27 each time. All 4,349,409 consecutive events of the run in this layout follow it.

At a change of era a carry runs from Z through C into R and R gets a digit more; C loses one, X gains one, and twice N gives its two lowest digits to the words on the right. How the new values are made is not decoded yet. If C keeps losing a digit per era, the layout has to change within a few more eras. No rule of the cascade or of the X layer can halt.

sections.heading: One law for every era
html:
All the layouts of the run, the plain cascade, the X layer and everything after, are one shape: Z followed by a chain of binary words, alternately of two kinds (W with digits 0001, 0101 and U with digits 1000, 1010), separated by the blocks 1 1, 0 1 and 1 0 1 1, any of them possibly empty:

0∞ 1 0 [N] A> 0 [Z] 1 1 [W₁] 0 1 [U₁] 1 0 1 1 [W₂] 0 1 [U₂] … 1 0 1 1 [Wm] 0 1 [Um] 0∞

Every word is a binary counter, and every wrap sends 3 to the next word. Each event adds 1 to Z; when Z wraps, W₁ gets 3; when W₁ wraps, U₁ gets 3; and so on. An empty word wraps at once, so it passes 3 times what it got. In one number: Z + 2|Z|/3 · (W₁ + 2|W₁|/3 · (U₁ + …)) grows by exactly 1 per event. The rules of the earlier sections are special cases: the cascade is one pair (C, R), the X layer two pairs (∅, X) and (C, R), and for the X layer the law gives the odd-looking C + 24/2k (an empty W makes the 3 into 9, X of k digits takes 9 mod 2k and passes the rest on, times 3).

The law is proved in Lean for every number of words and every width (lean/Layers.lean), from 23 visit rows of blocks of 1, 2 and 4 cells composed by induction.

Because the right side is one counter, a simulator can jump straight to the last event before a carry would leave the last word, and run only the change of era cell by cell. The first eras of the run:

sections.heading: What is left
html: The engine is proved for every layout: N + 1 on the left, and on the right the chain law. A halt can only come during a change of era, when a carry runs off the last word: every event that follows the law is a run of the machine that never reads the halting 1. At the end of an era all words are near their largest values; after the change they hold small values, the boundaries between words have moved by a digit, the last word has a digit more, and N has either gained 1 or given 2 to 9 of its lowest base-3 digits to new words. Open: (1) a rule for this hand-over; (2) whether some change of era can ever put the head on the halting 1.

sections.heading: One visit of a stream
html: Cut the tape right of the event cell into tokens of two cells: z = 00, a = 10, c = 01. Everything from R on, the blank tape included, is one stream of a and z, and one visit of the head in state B does this to it: the first z becomes a, and every second a before it becomes z.

If the first z is at an odd place the visit comes out in state A: with digits a z = 0 and a a = 1 this is the binary increment of R. If it is at an even place (all digits 1 up to the blank tape) the visit comes out in state C and leaves the digits shifted by one token. So R has no overflow into something else; the rare case is a visit that comes out in C.

Both cases, and M's increment and wrap (three visits of the stream), are proved in Lean for every size from 29 token rows, each of which is a small theorem about one token and the nested visits of the rest. What the c tokens of M do after a visit that comes out in C is in those rows but not yet composed; that is where the question of halting now sits.

summary: Two-word sweeper: a base-3 counter N and a chain of binary words; each event adds 1 to N and to Z, and each wrap of a word sends 3 to the next (proved in Lean for every layout). The run has been followed through 510 changes of era (2.4·10^297 events) with no halt; the era changes are open.
